title: Testing with floats
objectives: Explain why `==` on floats makes a test fail on correct code
Choose relative or absolute tolerance for returns and money

screens.title: Exactly 10%
screens.prose: A share rises from £10.10 to £11.11. On paper that is £1.01 on £10.10, exactly 10%. You write the test the obvious way.
screens.question: `simple_return` is correct. Does the test pass?

options.why: You did the sum on paper, where it is exact. In floats the code gives 0.09999999999999998.
Dividing two floats is fine. The code returns a number, just not quite 0.1.

hints.text: Can a float hold 10.10 or 11.11 exactly?
Neither price is stored exactly, so their difference is a hair off £1.01, and the return a hair off 0.1.

feedback.correct: Right code, failed test: the float is a hair below 0.1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about how floats store 10.10 and 11.11.

explain.text: pytest reports `assert 0.09999999999999998 == 0.1`. Neither price is stored exactly in binary, so the result misses 0.1 by about 2.8e−17. The code is right; the test demands an exactness floats cannot give.

screens.prose: Instead of exact equality, accept any result within a **tolerance** of 0.1. The table holds the right code's float result and a real bug's result. Drag the tolerance from tiny to large and read the caption.

controls.label: Tolerance, as a power of ten

derive.caption: Tolerance 1e{{tol}}: right code {{2.8 * pow(10, -17) <= pow(10, tol) ? "passes" : "fails"}}, bug {{0.0091 <= pow(10, tol) ? "passes" : "fails"}}

screens.question: Which tolerances let the right code pass and still fail the bug?

options.why: At 1e−18 the right code fails too: its gap, 2.8e−17, is larger.
At 1e−1 the bug passes too: its gap, 0.0091, is smaller.
Drag through the middle. From 1e−16 to 1e−3 the right code passes and the bug fails.

hints.text: Compare each tolerance with the two gaps, 2.8e−17 and 0.0091.

feedback.correct: A wide band of tolerances separates a rounding slip from a real bug.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A tolerance must be above 2.8e−17 and below 0.0091.

explain.text: A rounding slip is around 1e−17, while a real bug moves the answer in the second or third decimal place. Any tolerance between them tells the two apart. That gap is why comparing within a tolerance is safe.

screens.prose: pytest does this for you. `x == pytest.approx(0.1)` is True when `x` is within a millionth of 0.1, relative to 0.1. That tolerance sits in the safe band you found.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which of these asserts pass?

options.why: A gap of 0.0091 is about 9% of 0.1. approx allows a millionth.
A gap of 0.01 is 10% of 0.1, far beyond a millionth.

hints.text: A millionth of 0.1 is 1e−7. Which gaps are smaller than that?
An exact match has a gap of zero.

feedback.correct: The slip and the exact value pass. Both real misses fail.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each gap with a millionth of 0.1, which is 1e−7.

byKey.exact: An exact 0.1 passes too: a gap of zero is within any tolerance.

explain.text: A millionth of 0.1 is 1e−7. The slip of 2.8e−17 is far inside it, and an exact match has no gap at all. The misses of 0.0091 and 0.01 are far outside.

screens.prose:
The tolerance is **relative**: a millionth of the expected value. A test checks a fund's book value:

```python
assert book_value(holdings) == pytest.approx(1250000.00)
```
screens.question: How large a gap, in pounds, does `pytest.approx` allow here?

hints.text: Multiply the expected value by the relative tolerance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply £1,250,000.00 by one millionth.

byKey.abs: You took a millionth as a fixed gap. It is a millionth of the expected value, which here is £1.25.
byKey.tenth: You moved the decimal point one place too far. £1,250,000.00 × 0.000001 is £1.25.
byKey.big: You moved the decimal point one place the other way. A millionth of £1,250,000.00 is £1.25.

explain.text: £1,250,000.00 × 1e−6 = £1.25, so a pricing bug of £1.00 would pass. On money you often want a fixed gap instead: `pytest.approx(1250000.00, abs=0.005)` allows half a penny. The `rel=` and `abs=` arguments set each kind of gap.

screens.prose:
Three trades should net to zero. In floats the P&L comes out as `0.10 + 0.20 - 0.30`, which is `5.551115123125783e-17`, not 0.0.

```python
assert pnl == pytest.approx(0.0)
```
screens.question: Does the assert pass?

options.text: Yes: near zero, approx also allows a fixed gap of 1e−12
No: a millionth of 0 is 0, so only exactly 0.0 passes
options.why: You applied the relative rule alone. approx also has a fixed floor of 1e−12, for exactly this case.

options.text: No: approx refuses an expected value of 0
options.why: approx accepts 0. Near zero it falls back on its fixed gap of 1e−12.

options.text: Yes: approx ignores anything below a penny
options.why: The floor is 1e−12, far below a penny. `0.001 == pytest.approx(0.0)` fails.

hints.text: A relative tolerance of 0 would accept nothing. pytest adds a second, fixed gap.
approx allows the larger of a millionth of the expected value and 1e−12. Here that is 1e−12, and 5.6e−17 is smaller.

feedback.correct: 5.6e−17 is inside the fixed floor of 1e−12.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Near zero the relative gap vanishes, so think about what else approx allows.

explain.text: approx allows the larger of $10^{-6}$ times the expected value and $10^{-12}$. With an expected 0.0 that is $10^{-12}$, so the slip passes. This is the edge case of approx: an expected value of zero.

screens.prose:
A colleague rewrites `simple_return` as `return p1 / p0 - 1`. On paper it is the same formula. An old test, which used to pass, now fails:

```python
assert simple_return(100.00, 110.00) == 0.1
```
screens.question: What is wrong?

options.text: The test: `==` demanded one exact float, and the new formula rounds differently
The new formula: it gives the wrong return
options.why: You trusted the failing test. $p_1/p_0 - 1 = (p_1 - p_0)/p_0$ on paper; the gap is 8.3e−17, a rounding slip.

options.text: The prices: round prices should give exact returns
options.why: The old formula happened to round to exactly 0.1. The new one computes 1.1 first, and 1.1 is not exact in binary.

options.text: Nothing: rerun and it will pass
options.why: Floats are deterministic. The same formula gives the same 0.10000000000000009 every time.

hints.text: Is $p_1/p_0 - 1$ the same as $(p_1 - p_0)/p_0$ on paper?
Look at the size of the gap in the last column.
The gap is 8.3e−17. The code is right; only an exact comparison could fail on that.

feedback.correct: A correct refactor broke an exact test. The test was fragile all along.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide whether 0.10000000000000009 is a bug or a rounding slip.

byKey.code: You trusted the failing test. The two formulas agree on paper, and the gap of 8.3e−17 is a rounding slip.

explain.text: `110.00 / 100.00` is 1.1, which binary stores a hair high, so subtracting 1 leaves 0.10000000000000009. The code did not change its meaning, only its rounding. With `pytest.approx(0.1)` the test passes both versions and still catches real bugs.

canvas.caption: Gap 8.3e−17: a rounding slip, not a bug

screens.prose: Write a test that survives that refactor. The starter's first lines stand in for pytest, which this page cannot load; in your project you write `import pytest` instead.
screens.question: Write `test_ten_percent_rise` for £10.10 to £11.11 with `pytest.approx`.

tests.setup: simple_return = lambda p0, p1: (p1 - p0) / p0
simple_return = lambda p0, p1: p1 / p0 - 1
simple_return = lambda p0, p1: (p1 - p0) / p1
simple_return = lambda p0, p1: p1 / p0
simple_return = lambda p0, p1: (p0 - p1) / p0
simple_return = lambda p0, p1: (p1 - p0) / p0 * 100

widget.how: Check runs your test against both correct formulas, `(p1 - p0) / p0` and `p1 / p0 - 1`, where it must pass. Then against four broken versions, where it must fail.

hints.text: The hand answer is 0.1. Compare with it through `pytest.approx`.

feedback.correct: Your test passes both correct formulas and fails all four bugs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read which version your test let through or rejected.

byKey.test-1: Your test fails on the right code. With `==`, the float 0.09999999999999998 is not 0.1: use `pytest.approx(0.1)`.
byKey.test-2: Your test fails on the refactored formula, which gives 0.10000000000000009. Compare with `pytest.approx(0.1)`.
byKey.test-3: The version that divides by £11.11 got through. Your tolerance is too loose: keep approx's default.
byKey.test-5: The version with the sign flipped got through. Check the value, not just its size.
byKey.error: Your code stopped before the tests could run. Read the error under the editor.

explain.text:
Both formulas land within a millionth of 0.1, so the test passes either way. The bugs miss by at least 9%, so they still fail. The test now checks the meaning of the code, not its rounding.

```python
def test_ten_percent_rise():
    assert simple_return(10.10, 11.11) == pytest.approx(0.1)
```

screens.prose:
Whenever a result is a float, compare it with `pytest.approx`:

```python
import pytest

def test_ten_percent_rise():
    assert simple_return(10.10, 11.11) == pytest.approx(0.1)
```

The default gap is the larger of $10^{-6}$ times the expected value and $10^{-12}$. `rel=` and `abs=` change it. approx also takes a list.
screens.question: Which line compares a list of returns correctly?

options.why: The `==` inside runs first and compares exactly. approx then wraps a True or False.
`round` takes one number, not a list, so this raises `TypeError`.
That is exact equality again, element by element. One rounding slip fails it.

hints.text: Where does approx go in the single-number version?
On the right of `==`, wrapping the expected value. For a list, wrap the whole expected list.

feedback.correct: Wrap the expected list in approx, on the right of `==`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. approx wraps the expected value, on its own side of `==`.

explain.text: approx wraps the expected value and does the comparing itself. Given a list, it compares element by element, each within its own tolerance. Putting `==` inside approx compares exactly before approx can help.

screens.prose: A risk report quotes **annualised volatility**: the sample standard deviation of daily returns times $\sqrt{252}$. Test it on two inputs you can work out by hand. Write the hand answer as an expression, such as `math.sqrt(0.0002 * 252)`, not a rounded decimal.
screens.question: Write `test_two_days` and `test_constant_returns` with `pytest.approx`.

tests.setup: annualised_vol = lambda returns: math.sqrt(sum(r * r for r in returns) / (len(returns) - 1) * 252)

widget.how: Check runs both tests against two correct versions, which round differently, where they must pass. Then against five broken versions, where at least one test must fail.

hints.text: For +1% and −1% the mean is 0. Each squared gap from it is 0.0001.
The sample variance divides by n − 1 = 1: 0.0002. Annualised vol is the square root of 0.0002 × 252.
`assert annualised_vol([0.01, -0.01]) == pytest.approx(math.sqrt(0.0002 * 252))`, and for a constant series such as `[0.003, 0.003, 0.003]`, `== pytest.approx(0.0)`.

feedback.correct: Both tests pass on both correct versions, and every bug fails one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read which version your tests let through or rejected.

byKey.test-1: `test_two_days` fails on the right code. Use the exact expression `math.sqrt(0.0002 * 252)`: a rounded 0.2245 is outside a millionth.
byKey.test-2: `test_two_days` fails on a correct version that rounds differently. Compare with `pytest.approx`, not `==`.
byKey.test-3: `test_constant_returns` fails on the right code. A constant series has no spread, so expect 0.0.
byKey.test-5: The version that divides by n instead of n − 1 got through. Check `test_two_days` against the sample variance, 0.0002.
byKey.test-9: The version that forgets to subtract the mean got through. Use a nonzero constant return, such as 0.3% every day.
byKey.error: Your code stopped before the tests could run. Read the error under the editor.

explain.text:
For +1% and −1% the squared gaps sum to 0.0002 over $n - 1 = 1$, so vol is $\sqrt{0.0002 \times 252} \approx 0.2245$. A constant series has zero spread, which only a nonzero constant can test. approx lets both correct versions pass despite their different last digits.

```python
def test_two_days():
    assert annualised_vol([0.01, -0.01]) == pytest.approx(math.sqrt(0.0002 * 252))

def test_constant_returns():
    assert annualised_vol([0.003, 0.003, 0.003]) == pytest.approx(0.0)
```

ideas: Floats round, so correct code can miss a hand answer by about 1e−17. `==` turns that slip into a failed test.
`x == pytest.approx(y)` passes when the gap is within the larger of $10^{-6} |y|$ and $10^{-12}$. It works on single numbers and on lists.
The default gap is relative, so it grows with the value. For money, set `abs=` to a fixed gap such as half a penny.
summary.trap: An exact `==` test can fail after a correct refactor, such as `p1 / p0 - 1` for `(p1 - p0) / p0`. Compare floats with approx.

quiz.prose: Two trades make £0.10 and £0.20. A test checks the total.
quiz.question: Which assert is right for this test?

options.why: You trusted `==` on floats. `0.10 + 0.20` is 0.30000000000000004, so this fails.
`round` with no places rounds to a whole number, 0. That is not 0.30.
The text of the sum is `0.30000000000000004`, so this fails too.

feedback.correct: approx accepts the tiny slip in 0.30000000000000004.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out what `0.10 + 0.20` gives in floats.

explain.text: `0.10 + 0.20` is 0.30000000000000004 in floats. `pytest.approx(0.30)` accepts it, since the slip is far below a millionth of 0.30.

quiz.prose: A test asserts `price == pytest.approx(250.00)`, with the default tolerance.
quiz.question: What is the largest gap from £250.00 that passes, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the expected value by one millionth.

byKey.abs: You took a millionth as a fixed gap. It is relative: a millionth of £250.00.
byKey.floor: 1e−12 is the floor for values near zero. Here a millionth of £250.00 is larger.

explain.text: approx allows the larger of $10^{-6} \times 250 = 0.00025$ and $10^{-12}$. So £0.00025 either side of £250.00 passes.

quiz.prose: `p` is a list of five closing prices.
quiz.question: Which assert is safe without `pytest.approx`?

options.why: A return is a float from a division. It can miss 0.012 by a rounding slip.
A sum of floats piles up rounding slips. Compare with approx.
A square root of a float is almost never exact. Compare with approx.

feedback.correct: A length is a whole number, so `==` is exact.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the assert that compares whole numbers.

explain.text: `len` counts, so it gives an exact whole number: five prices, four returns. Every other assert compares floats, which need approx.
